podcast.title: Sub Pop Financial Issues (1990)
podcast.body: Sub Pop experienced money problems, leading to them selling Nirvana to DGC for $75,000. This shift significantly impacted the production and release of the *Sheep* album. "Subpop ran into money problems, and then they basically sold Nirvana off to DGC for $75,000."

podcast.title: "Nevermind" Release Date (September 24, 1991)
podcast.body: Nirvana's landmark album "Nevermind" was released on the exact same day as the Red Hot Chili Peppers' "Blood Sugar Sex Magik," September 24, 1991. "Same day as Nirvana's Nevermind."

podcast.title: Impact on Music Industry (1991)
podcast.body: Nirvana's *Nevermind* arrived when rock was stagnant, characterized by an "overabundance of classic rock acts" and "hair metal bands that had stopped being amusing with their stupid power ballads," alongside "crappy phony pop stars like vanilla ice and millie-vinyl." The album acted as a spokesperson for angry and scared Generation Xers during a recession and the Gulf War, leading to alternative music becoming mainstream and turning the rock world "literally upside down." "After Nevermind, what was once alternative became the mainstream."

podcast.title: Move to DGC Records (1991)
podcast.body: Facing financial constraints from Subpop despite high hopes for the band, Nirvana signed a contract with DGC on January 4, 1991. Their decision was influenced by Sonic Youth's earlier move to the same label, with Kurt Cobain believing if it was good enough for Sonic Youth, it was good enough for Nirvana. "So on January 4th, 1991, it was announced that Nirvana had signed a contract with DGC. Now why DGC? Well, like Thurston Moore said, it was because Sonic Youth had chosen that company as their major label home."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: 1992 MTV Music Video Awards Altercation
podcast.body: The animosity between Nirvana and Guns N' Roses culminated in a backstage altercation at the 1992 MTV Music Video Awards. Axl Rose confronted Kurt Cobain and Courtney Love, reportedly telling Kurt to "keep his woman in line." Simultaneously, Nirvana bassist Chris Novoselic and Guns N' Roses bassist Duff McKagan were also arguing. "This boiled over to an altercation backstage at the 1992 MTV Music Video Awards between Axel, Kurt and Courtney Love."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: First Rehab Stint (1992)
podcast.body: Kurt Cobain's first trip to rehab was in 1992 after learning he was going to be a father. He stayed for several weeks, but the treatment was ultimately ineffective, as he resumed using drugs upon Nirvana's return from an Australian tour. "His first trip to rehab was in 1992, after he found out that he was going to be a father."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Reading 1992 Performance
podcast.body: Nirvana played the Reading festival twice, with their 1992 appearance being recorded and released as a live album. During this performance, Kurt Cobain was rumored to be gravely ill and was wheeled onto the stage in a wheelchair wearing a hospital gown. He then stood up unsteadily, went to the microphone, and the charade ended as Nirvana delivered one of their most memorable performances. "Their 1992 appearance was recorded and released as a live album. This was the gig where Kurt was rumored to be Deathly Ill and he was wheeled on stage in a wheelchair in a hospital gown. He got up, very unsteady, made his way to the microphone. Then the charade was over and Nirvana busted into one of their most memorable performances."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Royalty Dispute Post-Nevermind (1992)
podcast.body: In the spring of 1992, after *Nevermind* became a global success, Kurt Cobain decided to unilaterally rewrite the band's royalty arrangements. He demanded 90% of the songwriting royalties, backdated to *Nevermind*'s release in September 1991, and called Dave Grohl and Chris Novoselic "greedy" for wanting a larger cut. After "a bunch of fights," Kurt was eventually "bargained down to 75%" of all material on *Nevermind*. "Things got really heated, especially when Kurt called Dave and Chris Greedy for wanting a bigger cut."

podcast.title: Decline During 1993
podcast.body: The band's degradation throughout 1993 was attributed not only to Curcomen's drug addiction but also to the exploitative practices of their label, Geffen Records, which pressured them for commercial gain. Recordings from their *In Utero* tour show a band that had lost much of its "spark" and "energy." "la degeneración de Nirvana en esa época fue fruto de muchas cosas no solo de la droga adición de curcoven."

podcast.title: Kurt Cobain Possibly Contributed Guitar and Vocals to Hole's "Asking For It" (1993, Rio)
podcast.body: An unofficial version of Hole's "Asking For It" exists featuring a male voice on background vocals widely attributed to Kurt Cobain. It is believed to have been recorded at Ariola Studios in Rio de Janeiro in January 1993 when Nirvana was there for four days and Courtney Love was traveling with the band. The version did not appear on *Live Through This*. An official outtake from the same Rio sessions, a demo of "Miss World," appears on *My Body the Hand Grenade*. "It's not that big a leap to assume that the version of asking for it was also recorded during the Rio sessions."

podcast.title: Late 1993 State of Collapse
podcast.body: By late 1993, when Nirvana finally agreed to the MTV Unplugged session, the band was "completely devastated, exhausted, without energy, and on the verge of collapse." This was a stark contrast to their energetic and ambitious state in early 1993 during the recording of *In Utero*. "la propia banda llega a finales en 1993 completamente arrasada agotada sin energía y al bordo del colapso."

podcast.title: Quieter Evolution (1993)
podcast.body: By late 1993, Nirvana, particularly evidenced by their *MTV Unplugged* set, began to explore a quieter, more acoustic sound. This shift indicated a broader mutation within alternative rock, moving away from the heavier sounds of earlier grunge toward more subdued and melodic approaches. "Like Nirvana, on their MTV Unplugged set, we're getting quieter, more acoustic."

podcast.title: Rio de Janeiro Studio Sessions with Hole (1993)
podcast.body: From January 19th to 22nd, 1993, all three members of Nirvana engaged in studio sessions in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, to develop new material for their *In Utero* album. Courtney Love and Hole's drummer, Patty Schemel, were also present during these four days, where approximately a dozen songs were committed to tape. Given Hole's bassist was absent, the situation makes an actual Nirvana-Hole collaborative venture "fairly reasonable" to assume, especially regarding Kurt Cobain's rumored involvement on Hole's "Miss World" demo and an unreleased version of "Asking For It."

podcast.title: Admission to Los Angeles Detox Center (March 30, 1994)
podcast.body: Kurt Cobain officially entered the Los Angeles detox center on March 30, 1994. Reports from the center were positive, indicating he was doing well, his health was improving, he had a positive attitude, played guitar often, and received visitors. "El 30 de marzo, unos días después, ingresa oficialmente en el centro de los áncieles de desintoxicación."

podcast.title: Aggressive Call and Rehab Escape (April 1, 1994)
podcast.body: On the night of April 1, conflicting reports suggest Kurt Cobain received a very aggressive phone call from Kurt Ylov at the detox center, which may have contributed to his escape. Regardless, he escaped the center, took a plane, and flew to Seattle. "hay quien dice que esa misma noche recibe una llamada muy agresiva del cornylofa al centro de sintoxicación. podcast.body: Going into 1994, Nirvana, alongside Pearl Jam, was regarded as one of the "unquestioned biggest bands in America," reflecting their immense influence and popularity. "Going into 1994, Nirvana and Pearl Jam were the unquestioned biggest bands in America."

podcast.title: Discovery of Kurt Cobain's Body (April 8, 1994)
podcast.body: On April 8, 1994, an electrician installing a security device found Kurt Cobain dead on the floor of his home, which he shared with Kurt Ylov. Initially disbelieving he was dead, the electrician found a suicide note, then called the police who certified his death. "el 8 de abril de 1994 cuando un electricista entra en casa de Córkovend y de Córnilof y se encuentra Córkovend en el suelo muerto."

podcast.title: Drug Intervention (March 25, 1994)
podcast.body: On March 25, Kurt Ylov organized a drug intervention for Kurt Cobain, attended by Nirvana band members, Geffen record label executives, and two of his best friends, to address his heroin problem. Kurt Cobain was very negative about the process, and initially denied having a major addiction, instead claiming Kurt Ylov was the one with the problem. "el 25 de marzo, o cosas más tarde, Kurt Ylov decía hace una especie de intervención de las drogas para Kurt Cobain."

podcast.title: Dylan Carlson Friendship and Shotgun Purchase (March 30, 1994)
podcast.body: Kurt Cobain maintained a close friendship with Dylan Carlson. On March 30, 1994, Carlson accompanied Cobain to Stan Baker's Sports in Seattle, where they purchased a Remington M11 shotgun for $308.37. Accounts differ on whether Kurt directly paid for it or if Dylan made the actual purchase after receiving money from Kurt. "He was Kurt's best friend, and he was the guy who went with Kurt to Stan Baker's Sports in Seattle, on March 30, 1994, to buy a Remington M11 shotgun for $308.37. Actually, some stories say that Kurt gave him the money, and Dylan was the person who actually bought it."

podcast.title: Encounter with Duff McKagan and Death (1994)
podcast.body: After escaping rehab, Kurt Cobain took Delta Flight 788 to Seattle and coincidentally sat next to Guns N' Roses bassist Duff McKagan, also a veteran of rehab. Cobain refused a ride from McKagan upon landing, signed autographs, and disappeared. He then acquired drugs, returned to the room above the greenhouse at his and Courtney Love's Lake Washington Boulevard home, got high, and died by suicide, believed to be on April 5th, 1994. The news of his death broke on Friday, April 8th. "Soon, he was on Delta Flight 788 to Seattle, and by sheer coincidence, he was sitting next to Guns & Roses bass player Duff McAgan, himself, a junkie we have veteran."

podcast.title: End of Band (1994)
podcast.body: Nirvana concluded its run in 1994. Following this, Dave Grohl started the Foo Fighters in 1995, retaining John Silva as his manager through this transition and all subsequent developments.

podcast.title: Escape from Rehab (April 1994)
podcast.body: After reluctantly agreeing to an intervention by friends and bandmates, Kurt Cobain checked into the Exodus Recovery Center in Los Angeles. However, he stayed for only two nights before slipping out on the evening of April 1, taking a cab to the airport. "He stayed two nights but then slipped out on the evening of April 1."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Escape from Rehab (April 1994)
podcast.body: While at the Exodus Recovery Center, Kurt Cobain befriended fellow patient Gibby Haynes of the Butthole Surfers. On the evening of Good Friday, April 1st, 1994, at 7:25 PM, Cobain told an attendant he was going for a smoke, then scaled a six-foot fence to escape, despite being able to simply walk out under Exodus policy. "Instead, he scaled the six-foot fence and made a break for it, which was unnecessarily dramatic, since under Exodus policy, he could have just walked out the front door."

podcast.title: European Tour Cancellation (March 1994)
podcast.body: Following their performance at Terminal 1 in Munich on March 1, 1994, the remainder of Nirvana's European tour was cancelled. This decision was made because Kurt Cobain was deemed unfit to continue, suffering from bronchitis and a sore throat. The other band members, Krist Novoselic and Dave Grohl, also needed a vacation, with Novoselic returning to Seattle and Grohl remaining in Germany to work on a film soundtrack. "After that show, the rest of the European tour was cancelled."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: European Tour Cancellation (March 1994)
podcast.body: The remainder of Nirvana's European tour was cancelled after the Munich show because Kurt was too sick with chronic bronchitis and laryngitis. "After the show in Munich, the rest of the tour was cancelled. Kurt was just too sick to continue with what doctors called chronic bronchitis and laryngitis."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Final Show March 1, 1994; Death April 8, 1994 – The Vacuum That Reshaped 1994's Rock Landscape
podcast.body: Nirvana played their final concert in Munich on March 1, 1994 — Kurt's voice was shot, the band was exhausted, and the rest of the European tour was canceled. On March 3, he deliberately overdosed on tranquilizers in a Rome hotel room. On March 18, police were called to his Seattle house after he locked himself in a room with guns. He agreed to enter rehab after an intervention, then escaped. His body was found April 8. The news was read on air: "Nirvana lead singer Kurt Cobain shot himself to death at a Seattle home yesterday." The effect on music fans was profound and prolonged. The loss of Nirvana's central narrative created a temporary opening that Green Day, The Offspring, Blur, and Oasis each rushed to fill. "Kurt's death was extremely traumatic. And the mourning continued for months."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Intervention and Second Rehab Stint (1994)
podcast.body: On March 25th, 1994, an intervention by friends, family, and business associates convinced Kurt Cobain to address his self-destructive behavior and heroin addiction. He reluctantly agreed to try rehab again, checking into the Exodus Recovery Center in Los Angeles on Thursday, March 30th. "On March 25th, 1994, an intervention of friends, family, and business associates convinced Kurt that his self-destructive tendencies brought on by his heroin issues had to stop, so he reluctantly and angrily agreed to try rehab again."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Intervention for Kurt Cobain (March 25, 1994)
podcast.body: Nirvana bandmates Chris Novoselic and Dave Grohl, along with touring guitarist Pat Smear, participated in a five-hour intervention for Kurt Cobain at his Seattle home. This was an attempt by his wife Courtney Love and others to convince him to address his drug problems, following a previous suicide attempt in Rome. "This group included Courtney, his bandmates, Chris Nova's Selaj and Dave Grohl, touring Nirvana guitars, Pat Smir, and members of Nirvana's management and legal team."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Kurt Cobain's Death (April 8, 1994)
podcast.body: The discovery of Kurt Cobain's death occurred on April 8, 1994, just two months after Green Day's Dookie was released. This tragic event profoundly influenced the musical landscape, causing the "heaviness and bleakness of Grunge" to seem "a little too much" for audiences, thereby paving the way for the emergence of the lighter pop punk sound. "Two months after Duckey was released, Kurt Cobain was found dead."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Kurt Cobain's Death (April 8, 1994)
podcast.body: On Friday, April 8, 1994, Kurt Cobain's body was discovered in his Seattle home. Police reported that a man in his 20s was found with a shotgun wound to the head, and a suicide note was nearby. An electrician doing work at the home found the body through a window, leading police to break into a cottage above a detached garage where the discovery was made. Cobain had been recuperating from an overdose of painkillers and champagne the previous month in Rome. His mother mentioned he had been missing for six days and that she had advised him not to join the "stupid club of other rock stars who had died early." Initially reported as 28, Cobain was 27 at the time of his death. "The record company official says Nirvana leads singer Kurt Cobain shot himself to death at his Seattle home yesterday."

podcast.title: Kurt Cobain's Death (April 8, 1994)
podcast.body: The short answer to whether Kurt Cobain was murdered is "no." However, many conspiracy theories persist, citing "unanswered questions" such as how he could inject a massive heroin overdose, put his gear away, and shoot himself before being incapacitated, the alleged change in handwriting on his suicide note, who used his credit card post-mortem, and why a room above the garden house wasn't checked during searches. These questions have fueled documentaries, books, and websites. Applying Occam's Razor, the "simplest answer is usually the correct one." Kurt was described as a depressed, unhealthy, hardcore heroin addict who associated with "very weird and bad people," had an obsession with guns, and was "certifiably suicidal." His body was so accustomed to heroin that a fatal dose might have had a delayed effect, allowing him time to put away a syringe and aim the gun. The murder theory is deemed "just chasing shadows," though the possibility of being wrong is acknowledged. "My short answer to this is no. Now there are all sorts of unanswered questions. How did Kurt manage to inject himself with a massive overdose of heroin, put his gear away in the maneuver the shot got in time before the drugs knocked him out? What about the fact that the handwriting on the suicide note appears to change? Who was using Kurt's credit card in the hours and days after he died? Why didn't anyone think to check the room above the garden house when they were searching for him?"

podcast.title: Church of Kurt Cobain (1996) – Media Hoax Won a Contest to Fool The Oregonian
podcast.body: On May 29, 1996, a man calling himself "Reverend Jim Dillon" announced the founding of the Church of Kurt Cobain in Portland, Oregon, using Nirvana song lyrics as liturgy. The story received front-page coverage in *The Oregonian*, was picked up by MTV, and led the ABC Evening News with Peter Jennings. In reality it was a hoax — a local radio station had run a contest to see if listeners could trick *The Oregonian* into printing a fake story, and the winner was a man named Jerry Catel, who became "the Reverend Jim Dillon." His secondary intent was to make a statement about media shallowness and celebrity idolatry. "It was a hoax. The truth is that all this originated with a local radio station which staged a contest to see if listeners could get the Oregonian to print a fake story."

podcast.body: The short answer to whether Kurt Cobain was murdered is "no." However, many conspiracy theories persist, citing "unanswered questions" such as how he could inject a massive heroin overdose, put his gear away, and shoot himself before being incapacitated, the alleged change in handwriting on his suicide note, who used his credit card post-mortem, and why a room above the garden house wasn't checked during searches. Kurt was described as a depressed, unhealthy, hardcore heroin addict who associated with "very weird and bad people," had an obsession with guns, and was "certifiably suicidal." His body was so accustomed to heroin that a fatal dose might have had a delayed effect, allowing him time to put away a syringe and aim the gun. The murder theory is deemed "just chasing shadows," though the possibility of being wrong is acknowledged. "My short answer to this is no. Now there are all sorts of unanswered questions. How did Kurt manage to inject himself with a massive overdose of heroin, put his gear away in the maneuver the shot got in time before the drugs knocked him out? podcast.title: Suicide Runs in Kurt Cobain's Family Across Multiple Generations
podcast.body: Kurt's great-great-grandfather John Cobain was a county sheriff who accidentally shot himself in 1938. His great-grandfather James Irving stabbed himself in the stomach in front of his family in 1935, was institutionalized, and died two months later after ripping out his own stitches. His great-uncle Burl Cobain shot himself in the stomach with a .38 in 1979; when that failed he shot himself in the head. At age 14, Kurt told friends he planned to kill himself one day after becoming a rock star. At 15 he and his stepbrother James made a short film called *Kurt Commits Bloody Suicide*. At 13 he wrote in his journals of planning to actually kill himself. At 16, drunk and stoned, he lay on train tracks with a large piece of cement on his chest waiting to be hit; the train went past on a different track. The famous March 1994 Rome hotel overdose was the last major attempt before his death on April 5, 1994 (aged 27) in his Seattle home. "He said he had suicide genes."

Dave flew to Seattle, arriving on Friday, September 21, 1990, and after an informal audition, became a member of the band without any explicit invitation, simply because "they just didn't ask him to leave." xref.title: Attempted Suicide in Rome (March 3, 1994)
xref.body: Kurt Cobain was found unconscious on the floor of room 541 at the Excelsior Hotel in Rome on March 3, 1994, after consuming up to 50 Rohypnol pills in addition to alcohol. He had been suffering from extreme depression, calling Courtney Love numerous times expressing hatred for "everything and everybody" after a series of European tour shows were canceled due to a throat issue. Courtney Love flew to Rome to meet him; they ordered room service and champagne before going to bed. He was transported to Umberto Polyclinic Hospital for his stomach to be pumped, and later to Rome American Hospital where he regained consciousness. He left a suicide note that, according to Courtney, read in part, "My doctor says I would have to choose between life and death. I'm choosing death." This incident was widely seen as an attempted suicide, predating his actual death by just over a month. "Nirvana and Kurt Cobain, who very nearly died in room 541 of the Excelsior Hotel in Rome on March 3, 1994."

xref.title: Death by Suicide (April 5, 1994)
xref.body: Kurt Cobain died in the early morning of Tuesday, April 5, 1994, by suicide via shotgun, preceded by a massive heroin overdose. His body was found approximately two weeks later, on April 8. His family and friends were aware he was in trouble, especially after a previous suicide attempt at a hotel in Rome. On March 25, 1994, an intervention was held at his Seattle home with his wife Courtney Love, bandmates Chris Novoselic and Dave Grohl, touring guitarist Pat Smear, and members of Nirvana's management and legal team, lasting five hours. He seemed convinced to seek help and flew to LA on March 30 to check into the Exodus Recovery Center. However, he left on April 1 (Good Friday) by scaling a six-foot wall, flew back to Seattle, and disappeared. His final note, addressed to his imaginary friend "Boddah," was found in his pocket after he injected a large amount of Mexican black tar heroin and then used a Remington shotgun to kill himself in the greenhouse at his home. "He had injected so much heroin that he probably never even heard the gun go off."

He seriously considered quitting music entirely or joining another band, having received invitations from Danzig and Tom Petty. However, he realized he didn't want to be "just a drummer," as playing drums would constantly remind him of his time in Nirvana, a painful memory at that point. Butch Vig, who had produced Nirvana's "Nevermind," received the news during this initial meeting, causing the project to be temporarily put on hold. "They all met up in London on April 8th of 1994. Yeah, that's that's right. They met for the first time the day Kurt Cobain killed himself."

xref.title: Intervention Attempt (March 25, 1994)
xref.body: On March 25, 1994, Kurt Cobain's wife, Courtney Love, gathered a group of doctors and friends at their Seattle home for an intervention. The group included Courtney, Nirvana bandmates Chris Novoselic and Dave Grohl, touring Nirvana guitarist Pat Smear, and members of Nirvana's management and legal team. This intervention lasted for five hours and was an attempt to confront Kurt about his problems and convince him to seek help. "This intervention lasted for five hours. When it was all over, Kurt seemed convinced, and he flew to LA on the 30th to check into a rehab unit known for straightening out strong-out celebrities."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Intervention and Brief Rehab Stay (March 25-April 1, 1994)
xref.body: On March 25, 1994, an intervention was held for Kurt Cobain, involving Nirvana members Krist Novoselic and Dave Grohl, guitarist Pat Smear, management and legal team members, doctors, and drug counselor James Burr. The five-hour meeting persuaded Kurt to enter rehab, and he communicated his intention to rest and recover via his AOL account. On March 30, he checked into the Exodus Recovery Center in Los Angeles but departed just two days later on April 1, scaling a guard wall despite having checked in voluntarily. "That meeting lasted five hours. Kurt was convinced to try rehab and arrangements were made."

xref.title: Intervention and Rome Suicide Attempt (1994)
xref.body: By the end of March 1994, Kurt Cobain's family, friends, and business associates were acutely aware of his troubles, especially after a previous suicide attempt at a hotel in Rome. On March 25th, 1994, his wife, Courtney Love, organized a five-hour intervention at their Seattle home with doctors, friends, bandmates (Chris Novoselic, Dave Grohl, Pat Smear), and members of Nirvana's management and legal team, in an attempt to compel him to address his problems. "He'd already attended suicide once at a hotel in Rome, and people were afraid he'd try it again."

xref.title: Last Autograph (April 2, 1994)
xref.body: Around 1 AM on Saturday, April 2nd, 1994, at Sea-Tac Airport, Kurt was recognized by a Canadian Nirvana fan who asked him to sign a copy of Jane Austen's "Mansfield Park." The autograph was strangely dated April 5th, the day Kurt ultimately died. "The weird thing about this autograph is that Kurt dated it as April 5th, which is the day he ended up killing himself."

xref.title: Last Concert Performance (March 1, 1994)
xref.body: Kurt Cobain's final live performance took place on March 1, 1994, at Terminal 1, an old airplane hangar in Munich, Germany, attended by approximately 3,000 people. Despite suffering from bronchitis and a sore throat, and experiencing a power failure that necessitated a quick acoustic set, Nirvana completed the gig. This concert marked the end of his touring career, as the remainder of the European tour was subsequently cancelled due to his poor health. "No one knew it at the time, but this would be Kurt Cobain's last concert appearance."

xref.title: Final Concert (August 6, 1996) – The Palace, Hollywood
xref.body: The Ramones played their 2263rd and final gig on August 6, 1996, at The Palace in Hollywood, planned as a celebration of their career. By the 1990s, the band was finally being recognized as pioneers by alternative artists like Pearl Jam, Green Day, and Nirvana. The farewell included dates on the Lollapalooza tour that year, performing alongside Metallica and Soundgarden. Lemmy of Motorhead attended, and Eddie Vedder joined them on stage for their last song, a cover of Dave Clark Five's "Anyway You Want It." The band members simply walked off stage without a farewell speech after the final song. "That final show was on August 6th of 1996. xref.title: 606 Studios: The All-Purpose Hub (Northridge, California)
xref.body: In 2005, following the success of the "One by One" album, the Foo Fighters invested $750,000 to establish their 8,000-square-foot 606 Studios (also known as 606 West) in Northridge, California. Dave Grohl describes it as the "all-purpose Foo Fighters hub" where they rehearse, store gear, record albums, and host press events. The studio, originally a warehouse and once the home of a woman being stalked, was inspired by ABBA's Polar Studios and prominently features the recording console from the legendary Sound City Studios, used by Nirvana, Red Hot Chili Peppers, Rage Against the Machine, Slipknot, and Tom Petty. "By the time the Fuzc got to the one by one album in 2005, they had enough money to invest in their own recording studio in Northridge, California. They call it 606 Studios."

xref.title: Chronic Diarrhea and Self-Medication
xref.body: One of Kurt Cobain's notable symptoms was chronic diarrhea, which he regularly treated with the over-the-counter medication Imodium. xref.title: Feud with Nirvana
xref.body: The animosity began when Nirvana refused an offer to open for Guns N' Roses on a major world tour, a decision Kurt Cobain made due to concerns about being perceived as "sellouts" and his disdain for what he called the "typical Guns n' Roses type of band that has absolutely nothing to say." Axl Rose, a fan of Nirvana who even wore a Nirvana hat in the "Don't Cry" video, felt insulted and began publicly calling Kurt and Courtney Love "junkies," claiming their daughter had birth defects due to their drug use. "It began when Kurt refused an offer by the Gunners to have Nirvana open for them on one of their massive world tours."

xref.body: Unlike most producers who take a percentage of royalties, Albini charged a flat fee for his services. xref.title: Nirvana Dissolution if Alive
xref.body: Speculation suggests that if Kurt had lived, Nirvana might have dissolved undramatically, with Kurt pursuing his non-grunge, acoustic musical ideas, similar to later unplugged shows by Eddie Vedder and Chris Cornell. "maybe he would just sort of dissolve Nirvana. Not a breakup, but just an undramatic fade to black."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Nirvana Influence
xref.body: Both Craig Nichols and Patrick Matthews were huge fans of Nirvana, specifically drawing inspiration from the parts of Nirvana's catalog where Kurt Cobain stripped everything down to the basics. This foundational influence shaped The Vines' own musical approach. "Both were huge fans of Nirvana and wanted to do something like that. Specifically, the parts of the Nirvana canon were Kurt stripped everything down to the basics."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Revivals Part 4: Garage Rock

xref.title: Nirvana Role
xref.body: During his time with Nirvana (fall 1990 to April 1994), Dave Grohl was primarily the drummer, keeping time for Kurt Cobain's songs and singing some backup vocals. "Back in 1994, Dave was just the drummer. He kept time for Kurt songs and sang some backup vocals."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Nirvana and Pearl Jam Influence
xref.body: Like many bands of the era, Veruca Salt drew inspiration from the success of grunge giants such as Pearl Jam and Nirvana to begin creating their own music. "Like so many bands, they were inspired by the success of bands like Pearl Jam and Nirvana to start making their own music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Nirvana's "Nevermind" Inspiration
xref.body: His passion for writing songs was ignited by hearing Nirvana's album "Nevermind" for the first time, rather than his father's music, despite having learned some guitar and drums. "It was hearing Nirvana's Never Mind for the first time. He'd already learned a little guitar and drums, but it was that record that inspired him to start writing songs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Non-Conflicting Schedules with Nirvana
xref.body: A theory points out that there has never been any recording studio bookings or tour dates that conflicted between Weezer and Nirvana, suggesting that if one band was on the road, the other was in the studio, and vice-versa. "There never has been any recording studio bookings or tour dates that conflicted with either band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Opened for Guns N' Roses
xref.body: Soundgarden was chosen to open for Guns N' Roses on their "Use Your Illusion" tour, an opportunity that Nirvana declined. "They were picked to open for guns and roses on the Usur illusion tour"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Optimism vs. Grunge Pessimism
xref.body: Noel Gallagher intentionally infused Oasis's music with optimism, directly contrasting with the gloom and pessimism of grunge. He expressed annoyance at Nirvana for writing a song like "I hate myself and want to die," believing that even with nothing, life was "effing great." "Noel was particularly annoyed at Nirvana for writing a song like, I hate myself and want to die."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Origin from Nirvana
xref.body: The formation and existence of the Foo Fighters band directly followed Dave Grohl's time as a member of Nirvana. "now we're up to the time he joins Nirvana, which of course leads into the Fufighters, and we're done, right?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Past Relationship with Kurt Cobain
xref.body: Kathleen Hanna once dated Kurt Cobain. During this time, she famously spray-painted "Kurt smells like teen spirit" on his apartment wall in 1991, which inadvertently became the title of a Nirvana song. "and she once dated Kurt Cobain, which brings me to this story."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Pat Smear's Pre-Nirvana Band
xref.body: Before joining Nirvana as a touring guitarist, Pat Smear was a member of The Germs. The band's singer, Darby Crash, died of a heroin overdose in 1980, marking one of Smear's early experiences with bandmate loss. "And before that, he was in the germs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Perceived Feud with Nirvana
xref.body: Pearl Jam was initially viewed critically by Kurt Cobain, who considered them "careerists," too commercial, corporate, and appealing to "jocks." However, Kurt later clarified that the perceived feud was largely his fault and that he should have targeted the record company for pushing Pearl Jam onto the "grunge bandwagon" without their full realization or will. Eddie Vedder now agrees with Kurt's assessment of what was happening to Pearl Jam at the time. "That never was a feud. I slagged them off because I didn't like their band. It was my fault. I should have been slagging off the record company instead of them."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Pioneering Indie-to-Major Label Transition
xref.body: For the first five albums of their career, R.E.M. operated as an indie group before signing with a major label for their sixth album, "Green," and achieving international stardom with "Out of Time." "R.E.M. had been an indie group for the first five albums of their career."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Pioneering Recording at Reciprocal Recording
xref.body: Bam Bam made their first record, the "Villains" EP, in 1984 at Reciprocal Recording. This made them the first Grunge band to record at that studio, which later became famous for hosting bands like Nirvana, Alice in Chains, Soundgarden, The Melvins, and Mudhoney. "They used reciprocal recording, making them the first Grunge band to make music there."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Plagiarism Claim Against Nirvana
xref.body: Killing Joke's song "80s" (1985), co-written by Jazz Coleman, was observed to have a guitar riff strikingly similar to Nirvana's "Come As You Are" (1991). The situation regarding a lawsuit remains unclear, with conflicting reports on whether action was taken or dropped after Kurt Cobain's death, or simply considered but not pursued for financial/personal reasons. "Some sources say that there was a lawsuit, but that it was dropped after Kurt Cobain commuted suicide. Others say that even though they considered suing, killing joke decided not to take any action on copyright infringement for personal and financial reasons."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Post-Nirvana Feud with Courtney Love
xref.body: A significant feud developed between Dave Grohl and Courtney Love after Kurt Cobain's death. The first public evidence of bad blood was a 1999 interview where Dave Grohl, when asked for his favorite Hole song, replied "Teenage Horror" because it was "the one I know Courtney actually wrote," implying she didn't write others. Courtney Love subsequently attacked Dave in the media over legal disputes concerning Nirvana's music, accusing him of being sexually obsessed with Kurt Cobain and claiming he hired Taylor Hawkins as Foo Fighters' drummer because of Hawkins' resemblance to Kurt. "The first evidence I can find of some kind of bad blood was an interview Dave gave in 1999, a few years after the food fighters got going."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Post-Nirvana Leadership – Foo Fighters
xref.body: Following the death of Kurt Cobain, Dave Grohl surprised many by stepping out from behind the drum kit. He transitioned to the role of leader, singer, and guitarist for his new band, the Foo Fighters, demonstrating his skills as a musician, songwriter, and singer that many had not expected. "After Kurt's death Dave stepped up from behind the kid as the leader singer and guitarist of the foo fighters."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Post-Nirvana Musical Ventures
xref.body: After Kurt Cobain's death, Chris Novoselic attempted to continue his musical career with several bands, but none achieved significant success. "Chris Nova Selich, the guy everyone thought would be the person to carry on Nirvana's musical legacy, tried to keep things going with a couple of bands, but things just didn't work out."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Post-Nirvana Success – Dave Grohl's New Role
xref.body: After the death of Kurt Cobain and the end of Nirvana, Dave Grohl formed the Foo Fighters, taking on the roles of leader, lead singer, and guitarist. The band achieved considerable success, surprising many who hadn't realized the extent of Grohl's musical, songwriting, and singing talents during his time as Nirvana's drummer. "After Kurt's death Dave stepped up from behind the kid as the leader singer and guitarist of the foo fighters and Well, they've done okay, huh."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Posthumous Business Deals
xref.body: Courtney Love sold a piece of the Nirvana Empire to Primary Wave, leading to increased merchandising like t-shirts, action figures, lunchboxes, and shoes, and the company now manages future licensing of Nirvana songs. Courtney also authorized the publication of Kurt's private diaries and was involved in the documentary "Montage of Heck." "Courtney sold a piece of the Nirvana Empire to a company called Primary Wave, which explains why we see more Kurt Cobain t-shirts and action figures and lunch boxes and shoes."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Pre-dating Major Grunge Bands
xref.body: Bam Bam, with Tina Bell, was active and developing their sound before bands like Nirvana, Soundgarden, and Alice in Chains. Their early contributions to the genre were not recognized in the same way as these later groups. "Tina and Bam Bam were doing their thing before Nirvana, before Soundgarden, before Allison Chains."

xref.title: Producer Collaboration
xref.body: Steve Elveni, a producer/engineer known for his work with bands like Nirvana and The Pixies, was such a fan of Shadowy Men on a Shadowy Planet that he worked on one of their albums for free. "Steve Elveni, the producer slash engineer known for working with Nirvana and the pixies and so many more, liked shadowy men so much that he worked on one of their albums for free."

xref.title: Producer of Notable Albums
xref.body: Butch Vig is a renowned record producer who worked with Kim Gordon and Sonic Youth on their album "Goo" and famously produced Nirvana's seminal album "Nevermind." He also produced L7's "Bricks Are Heavy." "butch vig, the guy who worked with Kim Gordon and the rest of Sonic Youth on the Goo album, and the dude who had just finished helping Nirvana make never mind."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Producing Nirvana's Nevermind (Age 36)
xref.body: At age 36, Butch Vig was asked to produce Nirvana's *Nevermind* album, a project that "set him up for life" due to its monumental success. "before he was asked to produce Never Mind for Nirvana. That's set him up for life, starting age 36."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Prominence in Alt Rock Dance Clubs (Early 1990s)
xref.body: By the early 1990s, Ministry was among the artists whose music was regularly played in hundreds of clubs dedicated to the Alt Rock dance scene. These clubs accommodated people dancing to a wide range of alternative music. "hundreds of clubs devoting several nights of week, if not all nights of the week, to accommodating people who wanted to dance to everything from Nirvana and Nine-inch Nails to Ministry."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Prominence in Alt Rock Dance Clubs (Early 1990s)
xref.body: The Red Hot Chili Peppers were part of the musical landscape of Alt Rock dance clubs in the early 1990s. Their music was featured alongside other alternative artists in clubs that catered to a dance-oriented audience. "hundreds of clubs devoting several nights of week, if not all nights of the week, to accommodating people who wanted to dance to everything from Nirvana and Nine-inch Nails to Ministry and the Red Hot Chili Peppers."

xref.title: Raw Songwriting Process
xref.body: The material found for "The Home Recordings" soundtrack for the "Montage of Heck" documentary provided an extremely raw and vulnerable insight into Kurt Cobain's songwriting and performance as he developed music for Nirvana, even though much of it was deemed "unlistenable." "But what this did was give fans a really good look at what was going on in Kurt's head as he tried to create music for Nirvana. It's songwriting and performance at its most raw and its most vulnerable."

xref.title: Rise of Alternative Rock
xref.body: Pearl Jam was among the many bands that saw a massive increase in record sales and broader recognition following the breakthrough success of Nirvana's *Nevermind* in 1991. They were part of a wave of "formerly fringe acts" that capitalized on Generation X's growing appetite for alternative music. "More jam, Soundgarden, Smashing Pumpkins, Stone Table Pile, Chili Peppers, and dozens and dozens of other formerly friendjacks started selling records and contradictions by the boatload."

xref.body: Pearl Jam was a key band in the rise of grunge, which caused alt-rock to coalesce around hard guitar rock in the early 1990s, driving significant record sales and concert attendance.
